The Counterculture and the Movements

🔊 Read aloud: listen to this page
Mr. MagisterYour teacher
Today's Focus

What did the protest movements of the 1960s want, and how did 1968 shake the country?

By the late 1960s the largest generation in American history was coming of age. This lesson follows the student and antiwar movements, the counterculture, women, farmworkers, and Black Power, the riots in the cities, the breaking point of 1968, and the turn toward Nixon and the silent majority.

Objectives
  1. I will be able to describe the major protest movements of the 1960s and what each wanted
  2. I will be able to explain how the war, assassinations, and unrest of 1968 shook confidence in American institutions
  3. I will be able to evaluate the political reaction that led many Americans to turn to Nixon
Quick Check-in

A big, mixed crowd all wants change, but each person wants something different. Who should the leaders listen to first? (No wrong answer. Just check in with yourself.)

The Book

⚡ DECIDE FIRST
Some Americans read the counterculture as a hunt for a kinder, more open way to live. Others read it as a turn against the work, family, and faith that a republic leans on.
Which worry weighs more with you, and what would you want to know before deciding? Decide first and jot down your answer before you open this.
The lesson gives a reason to take each view seriously, and also a caution: the protests were varied, some had little to do with politics, and many Americans, probably most, took no part in any of them. So a careful historian would ask how many people each view really describes. Critics worried about the bonds between citizens. Defenders pointed to a wish for peace and a gentler life. You can hold both thoughts at once, and the question stays open.
⚡ ONE MOVEMENT OR MANY?
How united were the protest movements of the 1960s?

    Verdict

    Could America Have Won?

    My Verdict

    1.The lesson says Nixon won office promising "law and order" and an honorable end to the war, while protests and the loss of public trust grew. Decide whether America could have won in Vietnam, or only under conditions you name, and say what "won" would have meant. Defend your verdict with one fact from the book that supports your view and one fact that cuts against it.

    The chapters describe antiwar protests that grew with the war and the draft, the shock of 1968, Nixon's appeal to a silent majority who supported the country, the deaths at Kent State, and trust in government falling from about three of every four Americans in 1964 to about half in 1970. They also say that most Americans took no part in the protests, and that Nixon was right that the silent majority existed.

    My Notebook
    Keep This in Mind

    The 1960s brought student, antiwar, women's, farmworker, and Black Power movements, a counterculture, riots, and the shocks of 1968. Many Americans answered by turning to Nixon and the silent majority, and trust in government fell.

    The Counterculture and the Movements

    Part 1

    Campus, Street, and Counterculture

    Chapter 1The Boomers and the Student Movement
    Chapter 2The Antiwar Movement and the Counterculture
    Chapter 1

    The Boomers and the Student Movement

    By the late 1960s, the largest generation in American history was coming of age. The baby boomers, about seventy-six million of them, had grown up with prosperity, television, and the Cold War, and many of them questioned the world their parents had built. At the same time, the nation was fighting an unpopular war and struggling with racial justice. It is not surprising that the decade became one of the most turbulent in the century. It is important to remember, though, that the protests were varied. Some were serious and aimed at fixing real problems. Some had little to do with politics. And many Americans, probably most, took no part in any of them.

    The student movement began at the universities. In 1962, a small group of young people met in Port Huron, Michigan, and wrote a statement of their ideas. They founded Students for a Democratic Society, known as SDS, which called for a politics of "participatory democracy" and criticized what its members saw as a cold and bureaucratic society. The statement had been written mostly by a student named Tom Hayden. In 1964, students at the University of California at Berkeley challenged a ban on political activity on campus. The ban covered a strip of sidewalk where students had set up tables for civil rights groups. In October, when police arrested a man at one of those tables, students sat down around the police car and kept it from moving for more than a day. In December, a student leader named Mario Savio told a crowd that the university had become a machine, and that they had to put their bodies upon its gears and stop it. Close to eight hundred protesters were arrested in a sit-in that month. The Free Speech Movement used sit-ins borrowed from the civil rights movement, and it began a wave of campus protest.

    Chapter 2

    The Antiwar Movement and the Counterculture

    As the war in Vietnam grew, so did the antiwar movement. Teach-ins, marches, and draft-card burnings spread. A teach-in was a day or night of lectures and debate about the war, and the first one was held at the University of Michigan in 1965. The draft gave the movement its sting, because young men who doubted the war faced the risk of being sent to fight it. In April 1967, the heavyweight boxing champion Muhammad Ali refused to be drafted, saying that his religious beliefs forbade him to fight. Boxing officials took away his title, and he was convicted of draft evasion, though the Supreme Court later overturned the conviction. In October 1967, about a hundred thousand protesters came to Washington, and many marched to the Pentagon. Soldiers with rifles guarded the building, and in one famous photograph, a young man slid a flower into a rifle barrel. Hundreds were arrested.

    A smaller part of the youth culture turned away from politics altogether. This was the counterculture, a way of life that rejected the habits and values of the older generation. Its members, called hippies, wore long hair and colorful clothes, experimented with drugs, listened to rock music, and talked of peace and love. The music of the age grew from the Beatles, who came to America in 1964 and drew a television audience of tens of millions, and from singers such as Bob Dylan and Jimi Hendrix. A former Harvard psychologist, Timothy Leary, urged the young to try drugs and drop out of ordinary life. In the "Summer of Love" of 1967, tens of thousands came to the Haight-Ashbury neighborhood of San Francisco. In August 1969, a huge music festival at Woodstock, in New York, drew about four hundred thousand people. Rain turned the farm field into mud, traffic stopped for miles, and the organizers gave up trying to collect tickets. Some saw this as a search for a freer and gentler way to live. Others, including many older Americans, saw it as a rejection of the work, family, and religion on which the republic depended. Even many who joined it admitted that it had a darker side. Four months after Woodstock, at a free concert at Altamont, near San Francisco, a man was stabbed to death in the crowd, and the mood of the age darkened. Many young people were hurt by the drugs they took, and communes, where people tried to live together without rules, often broke apart within a few years.

    Part 2

    Movements for Change

    Chapter 3Women Organize
    Chapter 4Farmworkers, Indians, and Black Power
    Chapter 5Cities Explode
    Chapter 3

    Women Organize

    Women organized too. The birth control pill, approved in 1960, had given many women a new say over whether and when to have children. In 1963, a writer named Betty Friedan published The Feminine Mystique, which said that many educated women were unhappy with a life limited to home and children. In 1966, Friedan and others founded the National Organization for Women, or NOW, to push for equal treatment. The 1964 Civil Rights Act had banned job discrimination based on sex, but it was not always enforced. NOW was born at a conference in Washington, where women who were angry that the Equal Employment Opportunity Commission, the agency that handled such complaints, was not taking the ban seriously decided that they needed an organization of their own. In 1972, Congress passed Title IX, a law that banned sex discrimination in education programs that received federal money, and its best-known effect was to open up school sports to girls and women. Before the law, fewer than three hundred thousand girls played high school sports. Today, more than three million do. Title IX was a lasting achievement. In the same year, Congress sent the Equal Rights Amendment to the states, but it fell a few states short of ratification: it needed thirty-eight, and thirty-five approved it. Women did not all agree, and some, such as the conservative activist Phyllis Schlafly, organized to oppose the amendment. Schlafly argued that it would take away protections that wives and mothers had under the law.

    Chapter 4

    Farmworkers, Indians, and Black Power

    Other groups pressed their claims. In California, Cesar Chavez and Dolores Huerta organized farmworkers, who were mostly Mexican American, into a union. The strike began in 1965, when Filipino American grape pickers in Delano walked off the job, and Chavez's group joined them. In 1966, strikers walked about three hundred miles from Delano to the state capital in Sacramento, and Chavez later fasted for twenty-five days to hold the movement to nonviolence. Using a nationwide grape boycott and a style of nonviolent protest borrowed from King, they won contracts in 1970. American Indian activists seized the island of Alcatraz in 1969, held it for nineteen months, and protested the treatment of tribes. They said that unused federal land should go back to Indians.

    Among Black Americans, a different voice was heard. After the Voting Rights Act, some activists said that the movement had to go further. In 1966, Stokely Carmichael, the leader of SNCC, called for Black Power, which urged Black Americans to build their own political and economic strength and to take pride in their heritage. He first used the words at a rally in Mississippi, during a march that continued the walk of James Meredith, who had been shot on the road. To some, the phrase meant self-reliance. To others, it sounded like a break with the earlier movement. The meaning was debated within the Black community as well.

    Chapter 5

    Cities Explode

    Meanwhile, cities exploded. In the summer of 1965, a riot in the Watts neighborhood of Los Angeles left thirty-four people dead. It began after police stopped a young Black driver and an angry crowd gathered, and the violence lasted six days. In the summer of 1967, riots broke out in Newark and Detroit, where forty-three people died and federal troops were called in. The Detroit riot began with a police raid on an after-hours bar. A commission appointed by Johnson, the Kerner Commission, blamed white racism and poverty, and warned that the nation was moving toward two societies, one Black and one white, separate and unequal. Many white Americans reacted with fear and anger, and some began to question whether the Great Society was working.

    Part 3

    1968 and After

    Chapter 6A Breaking Point
    Chapter 7Kent State
    Chapter 8How Should a Historian Judge the 1960s?
    Chapter 6

    A Breaking Point

    The year 1968 was a breaking point. In January came the Tet Offensive. In March, Senator Eugene McCarthy of Minnesota, who ran as a peace candidate, nearly beat Johnson in the New Hampshire primary. Later that month, Johnson said that he would not run again. On April 4, Martin Luther King Jr. was shot and killed in Memphis, Tennessee, where he had gone to support striking sanitation workers. The night before, he had told a crowd in Memphis that he had been to the mountaintop and that he might not get to the promised land with them. Riots broke out in more than a hundred cities.

    On June 5, Senator Robert Kennedy, who had just won the California primary and was a leading candidate for president, was shot and killed in Los Angeles. In August, at the Democratic convention in Chicago, police and protesters fought in the streets, with the cameras running. Outside the hall, police waded into crowds of protesters with clubs, and the protesters chanted that the whole world was watching. Inside, the delegates nominated Humphrey, who had not won a single primary, and many antiwar Democrats felt shut out. The party split. In November, Richard Nixon, a Republican who promised "law and order" and an honorable end to the war, narrowly defeated Vice President Hubert Humphrey. The margin was less than one percentage point. A third-party candidate, George Wallace, carried five Southern states and won nearly ten million votes.

    Nixon had a theory about who was on his side. Weeks after huge antiwar demonstrations in many cities, in a televised speech in November 1969, which you will read this week, he asked for the support of "the great silent majority of my fellow Americans." The silent majority meant ordinary working Americans who did not march or shout, but who went to work, paid their taxes, and supported the country. The speech helped Nixon, who was struggling to hold support for the war. Tens of thousands of letters and telegrams came in to support him. He was right that these Americans existed. The voters of 1968 and 1972 were drawn in large numbers to a message that stressed order, patriotism, and tradition.

    Chapter 7

    Kent State

    The antiwar movement had its own tragic turning point. In April 1970, Nixon announced that American troops had entered Cambodia, and colleges erupted. On May 4, at Kent State University in Ohio, National Guard soldiers fired into a crowd of student protesters and killed four. The Guard had been sent to Kent after protesters burned the campus ROTC building. The soldiers fired for about thirteen seconds, and nine other students were wounded. A photograph of a young woman kneeling and crying out over one of the bodies became a symbol of the day. Some of the dead had not even been protesting. Ten days later, two students were killed at Jackson State College in Mississippi, when police fired on a dormitory. In New York, meanwhile, construction workers attacked a crowd of student protesters, and later marched in support of the president. The nation was horrified. Many students stayed home for the rest of the year, and the sense of crisis deepened.

    Chapter 8

    How Should a Historian Judge the 1960s?

    How should a historian judge the 1960s? The classical republican looks at the bonds between citizens. In that light, the decade had real losses. Trust in government, which was high in 1960, fell steeply by 1970. In one survey, about three of every four Americans in 1964 said that they trusted the government in Washington to do what is right most of the time. By 1970, only about half did. The shared culture that radio and television had built in earlier decades began to break apart. On the other hand, many of the movements had pressed the republic to live up to its own promises, and they succeeded in several cases. The difficulty is that a nation can be both more just and less united. Nixon came to power on the promise to heal the divide. The next module shows how that worked out.
